options.content: **Replication Stream Health** — binary go/no-go signals for the standby stream. `replication_stream_stuck` is the most critical: any non-zero value means the stream has stopped making progress. `replication_stream_panic` and `replication_stream_error` indicate stream-level failures. `replication_stream_channel_full` indicates buffer pressure on the receiver.

panels.title: Stream Stuck
panels.description: Non-zero = stream has stopped making progress. Immediate alert.

panels.title: Stream Panics
panels.description: Rate of stream-level panics across all history instances.

panels.title: Stream Errors
panels.description: Rate of stream-level errors.

panels.title: Stream Channel Full
panels.description: Buffer pressure on the receiver side.

panels.title: Stream Health Over Time
panels.description: Timeseries view of all stream health signals. Any sustained non-zero value warrants investigation.

options.content: **Replication Lag** — how far behind this standby cluster is from the active. `replication_tasks_lag` is the headline: it measures the task ID delta between standby and active. Send/recv backlogs show queue depth on each side. **Note:** `replication_sender_rate_limit_latency` originates on the **active** cluster — elevated values here explain lag that has no visible cause on the standby side. The default `StandbyClusterDelay` is 5 minutes, so scheduled queue lag below 300s is expected baseline.

panels.title: Replication Tasks Lag
panels.description: How far behind the most-behind connected remote cluster is on this cluster's outgoing replication, as a distance in task IDs. It is not a count of replication tasks: every history task a shard creates, of any kind, takes the next ID from one sequence per shard, so the distance grows with all of that shard's task writes since the oldest position a remote cluster has not acknowledged. A cluster that is busy applying replication can read thousands here with no replication task outstanding. The server samples it on the cluster that holds the outgoing tasks, once per shard each time replication task cleanup runs (history.ReplicationTaskProcessorCleanupInterval, default 1m), and only when cleanup has something new to delete. For how far the standby is behind, read this panel against the active cluster, or use Replication Latency — Time Behind (End-to-End) here, which is in seconds and is the better signal. The gauge is the selected percentile of the samples from the last 10 minutes. Values above 100,000 show as exactly 100K, the top of the metric's buckets. Samples are few, so a high percentile reads close to the largest one; on a test cluster p99 sat at the cap for about 10 minutes after the clusters started and again after a standby outage, while p50 stayed low. Set the percentile to 0.50 to see the typical shard. There is no fixed healthy level, so compare with your own normal reading. Samples stop while a remote cluster has stopped acknowledging, because cleanup then has nothing to delete, so an empty or frozen gauge is not proof of health: check Replication Streams Received from Each Remote Cluster on the Temporal Server Dashboard. Earlier versions averaged the metric's sum by its count; that sum reads +Inf on real clusters.

panels.title: Recv Backlog Depth
panels.description: Average depth of the receiver-side replication backlog.

panels.title: Send Backlog Depth
panels.description: Average depth of the sender-side (active cluster) backlog. Emitted only by pull-based replication (history.enableReplicationStream false), so it is always empty on streaming replication, the default. On streaming replication, read Recv Backlog Depth and Replication Latency — Time Behind (End-to-End) instead.

panels.title: Replication Latencies
panels.description: End-to-end, queue, processing, and transmission latencies. On a healthy standby all should be low and stable.

panels.title: Sender Rate Limit Latency (Active → Standby)
panels.description: Time spent on the active cluster waiting on a server-side limiter before sending a low-priority replication task (history.ReplicationEnableRateLimit, default true). In every release through v1.32.2 that limiter lets every task through at once, so this panel reads near zero, and it is empty when no low-priority task is sent. Through v1.32.2, force-replication backfill is sent as high priority whenever transition history is on (the default from v1.30.0), so low-priority sends are rare. The per-stream sender limits, history.ReplicationStreamSenderHighPriorityQPS and history.ReplicationStreamSenderLowPriorityQPS (default 100 tasks per second per stream each), apply only when history.EnableReplicationTaskTieredProcessing is true; with it false, the default, nothing limits the send rate. Neither is measured by this panel.

panels.title: Replication Task Generation and Load Latency
panels.description: Generation latency = time from workflow event to replication task creation. Load latency = persistence schedule-to-start for replication tasks.

panels.title: Replication Latency — Time Behind (End-to-End)
panels.description: End-to-end replication_latency: wall-clock time from when a task is created on the active to when the standby applies it (server source: service/history/replication/executable_task.go). The p99 approximates how many seconds the standby's applied data trails the active — the single best 'how far behind is the standby' signal. Red at 20s aligns with alert FAILOVER-PRE-07 (handover blocker).

options.content: **Task Pipeline Health** — tracks the full replication task lifecycle on the standby receiver. The gap between `received` and `applied` on the throughput panel is your real-time backlog indicator. `task_errors_standby_retry_counter` is standby-specific: it increments when standby tasks can't find their history events and must retry — directly tied to `StandbyTaskMissingEventsResendDelay` (10min default). High attempt counts on the histogram indicate tasks struggling to apply.

panels.title: Replication Task Throughput (Recv vs Applied vs Failed)
panels.description: Received, applied, failed and skipped replication tasks per second on this cluster. On streaming replication, the default (history.enableReplicationStream true), the server does not emit the applied series, so that line is always empty and there is no received-minus-applied gap to read: use Recv Backlog Depth for the backlog. Applied is emitted only by pull-based replication. Sustained failed/s requires immediate investigation.

panels.title: Standby Retry Counter
panels.description: Increments when standby tasks cannot find history events and must retry. Tied to StandbyTaskMissingEventsResendDelay (default 10min). Sustained high values indicate the standby is consistently missing events from the active cluster.

panels.title: Replication Task Errors by Type
panels.description: Replication task errors broken down by error type. Useful for identifying specific failure modes.

panels.title: Replication Task Attempts Histogram
panels.description: Average attempts per replication task. High values mean tasks are struggling to apply — cross-reference with standby retry counter and stream health.

panels.title: Backfill and Duplicate Events
panels.description: Backfill rate indicates recovery is in progress (expected after a gap or restart). Elevated duplicate events indicate stream instability.

panels.title: Outlier Namespaces
panels.description: Namespaces that are disproportionately contributing to replication problems.

options.content:
**Replication DLQ** — where a replication task is parked after it fails to apply `history.ReplicationTaskProcessorErrorRetryMaxAttempts` times (default 80).

**This is not the history task DLQ.** That is a separate mechanism, governed by `history.TaskDLQEnabled`, covering history tasks that fail processing. Neither one is Cassandra-only: `replication_tasks_dlq` exists in the PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQLite schemas with insert, read and delete paths in each plugin, and every metric here is emitted from generic replication and shard code with no store gate. Versions of this dashboard before v2.3.0 claimed otherwise on all five panels.

**Reading these panels.** `replication_dlq_non_empty` is a counter incremented once per periodic check that finds a non-empty DLQ, not a gauge — the check runs roughly every 5 minutes per shard per source cluster with full jitter, which is why it is shown as an increase over a fixed 11-minute window. `replication_dlq_enqueue_failed` is the severe one: the task could not even be written to the DLQ, so nothing is preserved for inspection, and the write retries indefinitely. The two level gauges are task-ID positions, not message counts — task IDs come in per-shard ranges and are not contiguous, so the distance between max and ack tells you the DLQ is behind, not how much is in it. Count the real contents with `tdbg dlq`.

panels.title: Replication DLQ Non-Empty Observations (11m)
panels.description: Replication tasks that failed to apply history.ReplicationTaskProcessorErrorRetryMaxAttempts times (default 80) and were parked in the replication DLQ. replication_dlq_non_empty is a COUNTER, incremented once per periodic check that finds a non-empty DLQ - not a gauge. The check runs about every 5 minutes per shard per source cluster with full jitter, so gaps reach 5 minutes and any shorter window reads zero at random; the fixed 11m window guarantees at least two checks. Shown as an increase over that window rather than a running total, so it returns to zero once the DLQ drains. Above zero means something is parked in the replication DLQ right now. This is the REPLICATION DLQ, not the history task DLQ - history.TaskDLQEnabled does not govern it - and it is not Cassandra-only.

panels.title: Replication DLQ Enqueue Failures
panels.description: A replication task failed all its apply retries AND could not be written to the replication DLQ, so it is not even preserved for inspection - more severe than a task merely landing in the DLQ. The DLQ write is retried indefinitely, so this climbs fast for as long as the condition lasts. Reads replication_dlq_enqueue_failed; earlier versions of this dashboard read replication_dlq_failed, which does not exist in server source, so this panel never returned a point before v2.3.0.

panels.title: Replication DLQ Max Level
panels.description: Highest replication task ID ever written to the replication DLQ, across shards. Only updated at the moment a task is written, so it goes stale rather than falling - a flat line means no new dead-lettering, not an empty DLQ. Task IDs are allocated in per-shard ranges and are not contiguous, so this is a position, not a count of messages.

panels.title: Replication DLQ Ack Level
panels.description: Highest replication task ID acknowledged out of the replication DLQ, across shards. Compare with Max Level: while ack trails max, work is still parked. Task IDs are not contiguous, so the distance between the two is a position gap, not a message count - use tdbg dlq to count what is actually there.

panels.title: Replication DLQ Task-ID Distance (Max Minus Ack)
panels.description: Distance between the highest replication task ID written to the DLQ and the highest acknowledged, over time. A growing distance means dead-lettering is outpacing acknowledgement. Two cautions. Task IDs are allocated in per-shard ranges and are not contiguous, so this is a task-ID distance and NOT a count of messages - a large number does not tell you how many are parked, only how far apart the two positions are. And both series are a max across all shards and source clusters, while their instance tag is derived differently on each metric (the ack gauge tags the shard that owns the DLQ, the max gauge tags a shard id derived from the source), so the two maxima may not come from the same shard - treat this as a directional signal and confirm real contents with tdbg dlq.

options.content: **Namespace Replication** — separate from history task replication. Namespace replication failures are a distinct failure mode: you can have healthy history replication but broken namespace replication, which causes subtle issues on failover (missing namespaces, stale configs). Like the replication task DLQ, this one is implemented for every persistence backend.

panels.title: Namespace Replication Task Ack Level
panels.description: How far along namespace-level replication is. Flat line indicates replication has stalled.

panels.title: Namespace Replication DLQ Levels
panels.description: Gap between DLQ max level and ack level for namespace replication. Growing gap means namespace replication tasks are failing.

panels.title: Namespace Replication DLQ Enqueue Requests
panels.description: Rate of namespace replication tasks being sent to DLQ.

options.content:
**Standby Task Processing Behavior** — these metrics are expected to be non-zero on a standby cluster but spikes or sustained growth indicate problems.

`task_errors_not_active_counter` is expected on standby (tasks are not processed as active) but a sudden spike may indicate namespace misconfiguration or a stale active/passive assignment.

`replication_tasks_back_fill` indicates recovery is happening — expected after restarts or gaps, but sustained high rates mean the standby is consistently behind.

The scheduled queue lag baseline is ~300s (5min) due to `StandbyClusterDelay` default. Alert on growth **beyond** that baseline, not on the absolute value.

panels.title: Not-Active Task Errors (Expected on Standby)
panels.description: Expected non-zero on standby. A sudden spike may indicate namespace misconfiguration or incorrect active/passive cluster assignment.

panels.title: Standby Scheduled Queue Lag
panels.description: Scheduled queue lag on the standby. The ~300s (5min) baseline is expected due to StandbyClusterDelay. Alert on growth beyond baseline, not on absolute value.

panels.title: Task Terminal Failures and DLQ Failures
panels.description: Terminal failures = tasks that gave up after all retries. DLQ failures = tasks that failed AND could not be written to DLQ (most severe).

panels.title: Namespace Handover Errors
panels.description: Errors caused by namespace handover state. Expected during planned failover, unexpected otherwise.

options.content: **Standby Cluster Infrastructure** — the standby cluster's own persistence and shard health. Even though the standby doesn't serve live traffic, it still writes mutable state for replicated workflows. Persistence degradation on the standby directly impacts how quickly it can apply replication tasks.

panels.title: Persistence Latency
panels.description: Persistence latencies on the standby cluster broken down by operation.

panels.title: Persistence Errors
panels.description: Persistence errors on the standby cluster broken down by operation and error type.

panels.title: Shard Acquisition Latency
panels.description: Latency for acquiring shards on the standby. High values during failover prep are a warning sign.

panels.title: Shard Movement
panels.description: Shard creation and removal rate on the standby. Heavy churn during failover is expected; unexpected churn warrants investigation.

panels.title: Service Restarts
panels.description: Rate of service restarts by service on the standby cluster.

panels.title: Persistence Availability
panels.description: Percentage of persistence requests that succeeded on the standby cluster.

options.content: **History Scavenger** — Temporal's built-in cleanup for leftover workflow history: `history_tree` / `history_node` rows whose workflow execution has already been deleted. It runs about every 12 hours on every cluster, including this standby. **`scavenger_skips`** = branches skipped only because they are younger than `worker.historyScannerDataMinAge` (default 60 days); **`scavenger_success`** = branches handled without error — **kept or deleted** (not just deleted); **`scavenger_errors`** = branches that failed. If **skipped** towers over **handled** for short-lived workflows, the 60-day wait is blocking cleanup and this standby's history tables grow — lower `worker.historyScannerDataMinAge`. See the [XDC Standby Database Growth playbook](https://github.com/tsurdilo/temporal-metrics/blob/main/playbooks/xdc-standby-database-growth.md).

panels.title: Scavenger Activity — Skipped vs Handled
panels.description: Per-branch rates from the history scavenger on this cluster. 'skipped' = branches younger than worker.historyScannerDataMinAge (default 60d) left untouched; 'handled' = branches processed without error (kept OR deleted). When skipped dwarfs handled, the 60-day wait is blocking cleanup and history_tree/history_node grow. Lower worker.historyScannerDataMinAge to let the scavenger reclaim leftovers.

panels.title: Scavenger Errors
panels.description: Rate of branches the scavenger failed to process (couldn't read the branch, or the mutable-state lookup / history-branch delete failed). Should sit at ~0. A sustained non-zero rate is a different problem from the 60-day wait: cleanup is stalling because the scavenger's operations are erroring.
